newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia campaign enlivened by opposition alliance.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia campaign enlivened by opposition alliance.

text.p: Indonesia's general election campaign has been lacklustre so far and the only interesting feature has been a tentative alliance among groups opposed to the ruling Golkar party, political analysts said.
The analysts said in interviews with Reuters midway through the campaign for the May 29 parliamentary elections that Golkar's overwhelming advantage was not in doubt.
The only question, they said, was whether the party could attain its target of 70 percent of the vote.

But an alignment between the minority Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) and supporters of ousted minority party leader Megawati Sukarnoputri could spell the beginning of a two-party system in Indonesian politics, they said.
President Suharto's tightly-controlled political system allows only three political parties to contest elections -- Golkar, the PPP and the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI).

Megawati, the charismatic daughter of late founding president Sukarno, was ousted from the PDI leadership by a government-backed faction last year and her supporters have begun gravitating toward the PPP. The remnants of the PDI have had difficulty attracting supporters at campaign rallies.
"If you look at the campaigning of the PDI, you might say that it's dead," said columnist and independent analyst Alex Irwan. "That's a sign of the victory of Megawati."
But he added: "It's got nothing to do with the ballot counting in the end. That will be Golkar."
"If PDI becomes a non-entity, we are probably going to see more of a two-party system," said independent analyst Dewi Fortuna Anwar. "And the signs are the PDI will be routed."
Megawati has told her supporters not to participate in the campaign to protest against her ouster. As polling day nears, they are being wooed by the PPP.
Analysts say it would be better for them to vote for the PPP than to use the other traditional Indonesian way of voting against Golkar: "golput" or spoiling the ballot form.

"Megawati will not formally be able to say, 'Vote for the PPP'," said a Western diplomat. "But I think many of her people will be doing that unless told specifically not to. I don't think they will be told specifically not to. The alternative will be golput but she won't say that because it can be manipulated."

"The broader question is whether we are beginning to see a pro-government and con-government division in the country," the diplomat added. "It (the elections) will be a little more crystallised than in the past by virtue of the fact that you don't really have three parties but two parties."

But the analysts agreed that the campaign was lacklustre, especially considering that it provided the only opportunity for Indonesians to indulge in party politics. Political parties are barred from campaigning except during the alloted period prior to elections.

"In the past it's been much more exciting," said Anwar. "For the majority of the common people, elections mean you can parade on the streets and go round and round and obstruct traffic. It's a little bit of anarchy."
Irwan, the columnist, agreed, although both the PPP and Golkar have organised now-illegal parades through major cities.
"There is nothing like the campaigning in 1987 and 1992," he said. "The PDI could mobilise masses and that really pushed PPP and Golkar. There's no enthusiasm any more."
